title: Way to Win
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Win #1: Show up.*

The final standings are in. Mud Hens: two wins, ten losses. We are ninth out of ten teams, which means the Sunnyvale Sprouts, who have never once been sunny, finish last.

We sit at a round table at the Dugout Diner, where the floor is sticky with a specific kind of glue that feels like it has been there since the invention of breakfast. My dad orders milkshakes for everyone, and they arrive in tall, sweating glasses that look like they are about to slide off the table. They taste like someone squeezed a carton of milk and a bag of sugar into a blender and forgot to turn it on. I take a sip. It is thick. It is gray. I take another sip.

Abuela is leaning forward, tapping the table with a spoon. She has finally figured out offside, or at least she has decided what it means to her.

"I do not understand," she says. "That boy stands where he should not stand. It is rude. It is like interrupting a sentence. I want to call the league office. I want to speak to the manager."

"Dada, it's a rule," Dad says, holding up his foam finger like a white flag.

"It is a moral failing," she insists. She looks at me with the serious intensity of a judge who has just eaten a bad sandwich. "Did you stand where you should not stand, Dani? In the last game?"

I think about the final minute. I think about where I was standing. I was standing right where I needed to be.

"Yes, Abuela," I say. "I was very rude. I will write a letter of apology to the referee."
pages.image: A diner table with sticky brown surface, a tall sweating glass of thick gray milkshake in center, a small sharp-eyed grandmother in cardigan tapping table with spoon, a big loud dad in mechanic shirt holding foam finger, warm cluttered background.

pages.text:
My phone buzzes. It is Carter Boyle.

He has posted a new video. It is the last minute of the game. You see me take the shot. You see the ball hit the crossbar. You see the ball bounce off the ground and roll into the duck pond.

Then, the video changes. Carter has slowed it down. He has slowed down the moment Tank grabs the twins. He has slowed down the moment Josie hugs Priya. He has slowed down the moment I stand there, hands on my head, and then I look up and smile.

The trombone is still there. It is the same sad trombone. But underneath it, you can hear us breathing. You can hear the ducks quacking.

The comments are not mean.

Nia, who I do not talk to but who I used to sit with in third period, has written: "Best own goal ever."

I look at the screen. My thumb hovers over the keyboard. I type: "Best team ever."

I send it. I close the app. I do not open it again. I pick up my milkshake. It is getting warm. It tastes like cold metal and regret.
pages.image: A smartphone screen showing a paused video of kids hugging on a soccer field, a blurred background of a muddy pitch and a duck pond, a hand holding the phone, warm indoor lighting, soft focus.

pages.text:
Coach Gin is at the bus depot.

She stands by the door of her yellow bus, packing her things into a duffel bag. There is the steel thermos, the lanyard with the whistle and the bus key, and that fluorescent yellow windbreaker she never takes off.

She does not say goodbye. She does not say I love you, Mud Hens. She does not even offer good luck.

Instead, she zips the bag shut and looks directly at me.

"You did the work," she says.

She means the practice. She means the Loss Log turning into a Strategy Log. She means the sock with the true thing inside. She means the silence during that scrimmage when we finally stopped shouting at each other.

I reach into my pocket. I pull out the yellow armband. I have not taken it off since game one, not once, not even for sleep. I hold it out to her with both hands.

"Here," I say. "You can have it."

She looks at the fabric, then she looks at me.

"It is not the armband," she says. Her voice is quiet. It is the tone she uses when she is telling the truth. "You know that."

"I know," I say.

I put the armband back in my pocket.
pages.image: A silver-braided woman in a yellow windbreaker zipping a duffel bag next to a large big blank yellow minibus, a young girl in a red jersey holding a yellow armband, a steel thermos on the ground, early morning light, dusty depot floor.

pages.text:
It is dusk, and the light outside my window has turned the dull purple of a scraped knee.

I sit in my room and open the red notebook. I have written fifty-one ways to lose, and I read them all.

Way to Lose #1: Show up.
Way to Lose #4: Kick the ball into your own net, then apologize to the ball.
Way to Lose #51: Miss the last shot.

These lines map out every time my worth depended on someone else, a catalog of every moment I was afraid, and a record of who I was when I felt empty.

I turn to the last page, which is blank.

I pick up my pen. I do not write a joke, a stat, or a rating. I write one sentence. It is plain. It is short. It is true.

"The score is what happened. I am who I am."

I close the notebook. It feels heavy in my hand, solid and real, like a textbook I actually had to carry.

I stand up and walk to my closet. I take out the red jersey and put it on. Then I take the yellow armband out of my pocket and slide it onto my arm. It fits. It is mine.
pages.image: A young girl in a red soccer jersey and yellow armband sitting on a bed, holding a red notebook, a pen in hand, a window showing dusk sky, a yellow elastic in her high ponytail, a quiet, calm room.

pages.text:
*Way to Win #1: Show up.*

I step onto the grass, the dampness seeping through my cleats as the twilight swallows the slanted left side of the pitch. The duck pond is a black mirror in the distance, and the ducks are either asleep or pretending to be, which is hard to tell when you are the only one awake.

I stand there, alone in the fading light, and the air tastes like cold mud and coming rain. For a long, quiet second, I am not the captain, not the star, and not the girl in the video. I am just Dani, and that feels enough.

Then a ball rolls out of the darkness, sliding across the wet blades until it stops at my feet. I pick it up. It is cold, round, and real.

"Okay," I say to the empty field. My voice is steady. "Next game."
